chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from a number of our companions, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd, from Jamīl, from some of our companions, from one of the two of them, peace be upon them, concerning:

A man bought a sacrificial animal and slaughtered it. Then another man passed by it and recognized it. He said: This is my badanah; it was lost from me yesterday. And two men testified to that for him. So he said: Its meat belongs to him, but it does not suffice on behalf of either of them.

Then he said: For that reason, the sunnah has proceeded with marking it and garlanding it when it is identified. So this does not contradict the first report, because it only counted for its owner, in accordance with what the first report contained, when the one who found it slaughtered it on behalf of its owner. But the latter report includes one who slaughtered it on behalf of himself and claimed it for himself, so it did not suffice for the first one. He is only permitted the meat because of the two witnesses according to the outward legal ruling.

key_terms.إِشْعَارِهَا: marking the sacrificial animal to identify it as dedicated offering
key_terms.الشَّاهِدَيْنِ: the two witnesses whose testimony establishes the outward ruling
key_terms.بَدَنَتِي: my sacrificial camel or large offering animal
key_terms.تَقْلِيدِهَا: garlanding the sacrificial animal as a sign of consecration
key_terms.تُجْزِي: it suffices or legally counts in fulfillment of the obligation
key_terms.نَحَرَهُ: he slaughtered it in the prescribed manner for a camel or sacrificial animal
key_terms.هَدْيًا: a sacrificial offering designated for hajj rites

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a lost hajj sacrificial animal is found and slaughtered by another person?
ai.summary: This report discusses the legal ruling concerning a lost sacrificial animal in hajj that is found and slaughtered by someone else. If the finder slaughters it for himself, it does not count for either party, though the claimant may receive the meat when ownership is established by witnesses; the report also explains the legal wisdom behind marking and garlanding sacrificial animals.
